newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU hopes Clinton re-election can settle trade rows.
newsitem.headline: EU hopes Clinton re-election can settle trade rows.

text.p: The European Union hopes to settle a series of debilitating trade disputes with Washington now that U.S. President Bill Clinton has won four more years in the White House, officials said on Tuesday.

"It has been difficult doing business with Washington this year," said an official of the European Commission, the EU's executive. "In any election year, in any country, domestic issues dominate the agenda.".

The pressure of ensuring re-election has been cited by European trade officials as the chief cause of a simmering row between the EU and the U.S. over Washington's Helms-Burton Act, which seeks to isolate America's arch-enemy Cuba.

Clinton passed the act -- an amalgamation of decades of Washington's anti-Cuba policy -- after Havana earlier this year shot down two U.S. light aircraft it said had repeatedly strayed into its airspace.

Although Clinton is known to have been privately opposed to parts of the act -- specifically laws which affect foreign companies -- analysts said he could not afford to give his Republican opponent Bob Dole an inch in the campaign.

Analysts said the fact he suspended the practical implications of the act until January despite it being passed by a Repblican- controlled congress suggested he might be inclined to try settle the dispute once re-elected.

However, the return to Congress of the act's chief sponsor -- Republican Jesse Helms -- as well as the failed attempt by the Democrats to wrest control of the House meant the issue would not be lightly solved.
Helms-Burton is not the only trade dispute that EU officials hope to settle with Washington in the aftermath of the election.
The EU has been at odds with the U.S. over European fur import restrictions, global semiconductor trade, business dealings with Iran and Libya and the telecoms industry.
The two sides are currently also at odds in Geneva where officials are attempting to thrash out an agenda for next month's World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting in Singapore.
Washington would like to see the issue of labour standards on the agenda, but the EU fears that will upset delicate relations with developing nations -- particularly those in Asia.
But it is Helms-Burton that looks likely to dominate relations in the short-term.
Stuart Eizenstat, the special envoy appointed by Clinton to win support for Washington's Cuba policies, is due to report soon on how his mission has fared.
Eizenstat's efforts have been publically rubbished by EU leaders, but analysts say now the bloc has its retaliatory laws in place the commission might be prepared to make conciliatory noises.
Nevertheless, the matter of an official complaint against Helms-Burton remains at the WTO where a disputes panel is due to be formed later this month.

An early further suspension of the act by Clinton -- it is due to come into effect at the end of January -- might persuade Europe to look again at the consequences of the WTO action, particularly as Washington has anyway threatened to ignore any rulings on the grounds the issue compromises national security.
